pr_title: chore/refactor(e2e tests): Solidify Contract for and Cleanup WaitForPodsRunningReady
pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind cleanup
/kind flake

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This cleans up the the test helper function `WaitForPodsRunningReady`. In particular, concretely defines the expected behavior for this function, rewrite to follow this expected behavior, and remove the log message that caused the original confusion.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
<!--
*Automatically closes linked issue when PR is merged.
Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.
_If PR is about `failing-tests or flakes`, please post the related issues/tests in a comment and do not use `Fixes`_*
-->
Fixes #111092

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This is an extremely simple issue that's remained open for a quite a while. With this being my first K8s PR, the simplicity was appealing to me! PRs have been opened to address this issue, but closed because agreement wasn't reached on how exactly to approach it. Of course, to agree on what to log, there needs to be clarity on what this function is doing. Unfortunately, I don't think the contract for this function has ever been well-defined.

Firstly, what exactly does it mean to have one parameter specify the minimum of Ready Pods, another specify the maximum number of Pods that are allowed to not be Ready, but also document that this function waits for all Pods are either Ready or Failed? I have no idea how that's supposed to work before reading the code! However, reading the code doesn't clarify much.

The clearest way to see the problem with the previous code is to consider: "What happens if every Pod in this Namespace fails?" The code will remain polling for the duration of timeout. Once it exits, then `notReady` will be 0, and this function will return without an error! *Surely* this can't be the intended behavior. This code has been refactored over the past few years, but this same problem has existed since this file was created 5 years ago. This is just one example of why this code is problematic- simply incrementing `notReady` for failed Pods wouldn't completely fix things in my mind.

Ultimately, I needed to decide what the contract for this function should be. I chose one that balanced similarity to previous behavior with what I felt is expected behavior:

```

WaitForPodsRunningReady waits up to timeout for the following conditions:
 1. At least minPods Pods in Namespace ns are Running and Ready
 2. No more than allowedNotReadyPods Pods in Namespace ns are not either
    Ready, Succeeded, or Failed with a Controller.

```

Once I established this, it became clear that a bunch of the logic was entirely unecessary. In fact, I felt like that specific log line from the original Issue lost its purpose now that the presence of non-Ready Pods isn't treated as exceptional behavior, and I just removed it.

One notable consequence of establishing this contract is that this function now exits earlier than it used to in certain situations (roughly speaking, previously a single non-Ready Pod in the Namespace would make the function continue polling until `timeout`). Considering how amgiguous the contract for this function was previously, there's certainly risk that some tests in some environments implicitely rely upon this function taking longer than it needs to. All pertitent Linux e2e tests seem to be passing when run against a local WSL cluster, and I suppose we'll see about the CI tests. I assume that this sort of risk is considered acceptable?

#### Update 4/14

Based upon feedback, I split `WaitForPodsRunningReady` into two functions:

1. `WaitForPodsRunningReady` is now substantially simplied. In addition to the above simplifications, I removed `allowedNotReadyPods` entirely, since it was unused by almost all of the callers.
2. A new function, `WaitForAlmostAllPodsReady`, which is equivalent in behavior to the previous `WaitForPodsRunningReady`. I just kept some light cleanup I did.

Notably, I opted to copy-and-paste code between the functions instead of trying to make it DRY. Since we're scared to touch `WaitForAlmostAllPodsReady` but have more confidence in what the semantics of `WaitForPodsRunningReady` are, it seems best to not couple these two functions at all.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
No

@aojea Agreed! :) Thankfully, all but one calls to this functions follow the pattern of:

1. Create exactly `n` Pods
2. Call this function with `minPods=n` and `allowedNotReadyPods=0`
3. Seem to be expecting that exactly `n` Pods are Ready after this function is called.

That is, my change should make this function more consistent with the semantics these callers are expecting. Of course, it's difficult to eyeball the code and completely confirm that none are subtely assuming that the full `timeout` is waited in specific failure scenarios, but that'd be more of a problem with the tests themselves.

The only call that I'd be a bit concerned about is the one which is used when setting up the suite in `e2e.go`, where this function is called for the `kube-system` Namepace:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f8930f980d2986f9e486b04c14c3e93e57bdbe12/test/e2e/e2e.go#L225-L237

The only reason that it's concerning is that the values of `minPods` and `allowedNotReadyPods` are configurable, and this is the only place where `allowedNotReadyPods` may take a non-0 value. It's conceivable that someone has configured these flags in their test poorly, and their tests aren't flaky only because this function simply blocks for the entire duration of `timeout` and doesn't always return an error when it should. But again, that'd be a problem with how the test is configured.

The following call to `waitForDaemonSets` should at least help to mitigate this concern.
@pohly @BenTheElder @aojea Anything I can/should do to push this along (no rush on my end, of course)?

What patrick said, every time we have some changes like this we end with flakes that take months to resolve or to root cause, starting with a new method and gradually migrate will help to roll out this change safely

@aojea @pohly Understood! I went back-and-forth on how much of a refactor to actually do, since I originally intended to merely fix the Issue about the logging. I can definitely appreciate that this amount of changes just doesn't seem worth the risk of dealing with flaky tests.

As suggested, I'll handle the single case which is more concerning that the others separetly. That will actually allow for even greater cleanup.

Thank you @aojea and @pohly 

As suggested, I split up the function `WaitForPodsRunningReady` into two functions, one of which is very close to the original and is only called when setting up the cluster in `e2e.go` and the other is substantially simplified and called everywhere else.

I update the PR description and added more comments explain the details of my decisions.

Thank you for the review @pohly. I addressed all of your comments. I've kept the change I made at the end of `WaitForAlmostAllPodsReady` for, but like I said I'm more than happy to remove if you'd like.

@pohly Thanks again for the comments, I reverted my change at the end of `WaitForAlmostAllPodsReady`, so that the function now behaves exactly as `WaitForPodsRunningReady`. I kept the couple of cosmetic refactors (no change in behavior) that I had made along the way, which I assume is fine.

review_comments:
This is almost identical to the previous `WaitForPodsRunningReady`. Most line changes are just cleanup/refactoring. The only actual change is the check at the end for whether to return an error, which I explain there.

This function is only called in the setup function in `e2e.go`, since that's the only place that it isn't clearly safe to change to cleaner function below.
I think that is where the function originally came from, dating back to 2016 and earlier. That E2E tests then used it just "happened".

I'm sure you're right! I looked through the history of this file for clues on how this function is actually supposed to work, but it's had the same basic structure since this file was created back in 2019 (clearly copy-and-pasted from some other file, but I stopped digging at that point).

Just to be clear (because the threading is a bit odd): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124205#discussion_r1568311204 is about "let's keep WaitForAlmostAllPodsReady exactly as it was before".

This variable used to be called `badPods`, but then was changed to `failedPods`. If it doesn't actually include all `failedPods` and just the one's we've decided are especially bad, then `badPods` seems like a better name.

This is a new function that is substantially cleaned up and simplified. Most notably, it doesn't even include `allowedNotReadyPods`, as I think that parameter was the source of most confusion and was only used by one caller (the call in `e2e.go`, which is now using the new function above).
One of the CI checks made me add these checks for errors
And for a good reason! The test was clearly broken without this error check.
Side note: in some cases I found tests that were no longer passing when adding missing error checking.

Agreed!

For the record, the fact that "failing to properly detect an error in this function constitutes the test that calls it being broken" is the reason that I thought it was important to fix the logic at the end of `WaitForAlmostAllPodsReady`. The logic for when the function returns an error is clearly busted, which is at least as bad as failing to check for errors.
